candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (trace a handover between people or services) and the porter's view of the moment of discharge led to following each handover as a person leaves the ward and asking which one goes to the family carer; stopwatch, cartography, rewinding and thresholds were not used.
candidates.working_title: The discharge handover to the family carer
candidates.core_insight: Discharge produces a letter for the GP and plans for pharmacy and home care, but the family carer who will give most of the care also needs a deliberate handover, and trials that built carers into discharge planning were linked with fewer readmissions.
candidates.angle: Treat the family carer as one of the recipients of the discharge handover, with the same care given to the GP letter: a meta-analysis of randomised trials found that discharge planning that integrated caregivers was associated with 25% fewer readmissions at 90 days and 24% fewer at 180 days.
candidates.position: Every discharge of an older person who relies on a family carer should include a handover to that carer: a written summary addressed to them, what has changed, what to watch for, who to call, and a supervised practice of any new task before they leave.
claims_needing_evidence: In a meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials in older adults discharged to the community, discharge planning with caregiver integration was associated with fewer readmissions at 90 days (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.91) and 180 days (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.90) (meta-analysis; abstract read this session).
The absolute readmission rates in the intervention and control arms of the pooled trials, so the effect can be stated as N in 100 (meta-analysis full text; PMC copy available).
NICE guidance recommends involving carers in discharge planning and giving them information and training for the care they will provide (NICE NG150; official document).
In Scotland, health boards have a statutory duty to involve carers in discharge planning (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016; legislation).
Family carers commonly carry out medical or nursing tasks at home after discharge, often without training (survey; US grey literature, check for UK equivalent).
evidence_leads: Rodakowski J, Rocco PB, Ortiz M, et al. Caregiver integration during discharge planning for older adults to reduce resource use: a metaanalysis. J Am Geriatr Soc 2017;65:1748-55. PMID 28369687. doi 10.1111/jgs.14873 (abstract read this session; PMC5555776).

candidates.opening_line_draft: A discharge usually produces a letter for the GP, a medicines list for the pharmacy and a plan for the home care agency. Ask what the family carer receives.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: an older man leaving a ward in a wheelchair with his wife beside him, and four labelled arrows to GP (discharge letter), community pharmacy (medicines list), home care agency (care plan) and family carer (an empty box headed 'What do they receive?'). candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (find the first question worth asking) and a son's viewpoint over three months led to the question an adult child can ask the parent who is doing the caring, rather than the parent who is ill; stepladder, restaurant kitchens, adjusting and distance were not used.
candidates.working_title: When one parent is caring for the other
candidates.core_insight: When one of your parents looks after the other, the parent doing the caring has needs of their own, and asking them directly, on their own, is the first step to getting them support, including a carer's assessment that does not depend on their income or on how much care they give.
candidates.angle: Family attention goes to the parent who is ill; the question worth asking first is to the parent who cares, and the answer can lead to a legal entitlement most families never use.
candidates.position: If one parent is caring for the other, ask the carer, away from the person they look after, how they are managing and what would help, and then ask the council for a carer's assessment (an adult carer support plan in Scotland).
claims_needing_evidence: In England, a local authority must assess any carer who appears to need support, whatever the level of that need and whatever the finances of the carer or the person cared for (Care Act 2014, section 10; legislation).

In Scotland, a local authority must offer an adult carer support plan to anyone it identifies as an adult carer, and must prepare one on request (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016, sections 6 to 8; legislation).
A carer does not have to live with the person or provide a set number of hours to be entitled to an assessment (Care Act 2014 and statutory guidance; legislation and official guidance).
Among unpaid carers in England and Wales, the proportion providing 50 or more hours a week is highest in older age groups [N to verify] (ONS Census 2021 unpaid care release; official statistics).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (trace a handover between people or services) and the last week of life led to following who is supported after a death at home, which showed the home care worker falls outside the bereavement handover; hourglass, archives, signposting, redundancy and the trial designer's viewpoint were not used.
candidates.working_title: When a home care client dies
candidates.core_insight: Home care workers can grieve a client who dies, and in qualitative studies from New York and England they often lost paid work at the same time and received little acknowledgement; being told personally, support from peers and managers, and time to attend the funeral were what helped.
candidates.angle: Bereavement support is organised around families; the paid care worker who visited every day is rarely included, and for many the death also means lost hours and income.
candidates.position: Care agencies should tell a worker about a client's death personally and promptly, acknowledge the loss, and where the family welcome it, allow time to attend the funeral. This is a judgement supported by qualitative evidence, not by trials.
claims_needing_evidence: In a qualitative study with home care workers in New York City, workers described their grief after a client's death as disenfranchised by employer and social underestimation of the relationship, and a client's death often meant losing both a close relationship and a job (qualitative study; abstract read this session).

In interviews with 29 home care workers and 13 managers in England, caring for people with dementia at the end of life left workers emotionally drained and under-prepared; peer support, manager acknowledgement, time off and encouragement to attend the funeral were described as supportive (qualitative study; abstract read this session).

A substantial share of home care workers in England are on zero-hours contracts, so hours and pay depend on the clients on their rota [N to verify] (Skills for Care workforce data; official statistics).

candidates.gain: Specific actions an agency or family can take.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (find an outcome people value that the routine measure misses) and the viewpoint of a spouse of 50 years led to questioning 'time to care home admission' as the yardstick for carer support; lighthouse, bridge building, rationing, trade-offs and the first minute were not used.
candidates.working_title: A carer programme that worked without delaying the care home
candidates.core_insight: Carer support is often judged by whether it delays care home admission, but the UK START programme improved carers' anxiety and depression for six years without changing time to care home, and that benefit to the carer is worth having in itself.
candidates.angle: Two landmark trials: a US counselling and support programme for spouse carers was linked with a later move to a nursing home (a model-predicted median difference of 557 days), while START helped carers' mental health for six years with no clear difference in care home admission. Counted only by admissions, START would look like a failure.
candidates.position: Carer support should be judged first by the carer's health and quality of life. A later care home move is not automatically a better outcome, and an earlier one is not automatically a failure. This is a judgement about which outcome to value.
claims_needing_evidence: START was an eight-session, manual-based coping programme for family carers of people with dementia, delivered by supervised psychology graduates; 260 carers were randomised (RCT; abstract read this session).

Carer anxiety and depression scores (HADS total) were better with START at 24 months (mean difference -2.58) and over 72 months (adjusted mean difference -2.00, 95% CI -3.38 to -0.63) (RCT; abstracts read this session).
START did not show a clear difference in time to care home admission (intensity ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.35) (RCT 6-year follow-up; abstract read this session).

A US counselling and support programme for 406 spouse carers of people with Alzheimer disease was associated with a 28% lower rate of nursing home placement (HR 0.717) and a model-predicted median difference in time to placement of 557 days (RCT; abstract read this session).
What the minimal clinically important difference in HADS total score is, so the size of START's effect can be explained in plain words (methods paper; to find).

candidates.working_title: Count the faces at the door
candidates.core_insight: Home care is usually monitored by visits delivered, late or missed; the number of different care workers a person sees each month is simple to count from the rota and tells you whether the person is being washed and dressed by people who know them.
candidates.angle: Continuity of care worker is what NICE home care guidance asks for, and it is visible in data providers already hold, yet it is not usually one of the measures families or commissioners are shown.
candidates.position: Home care providers should report, and families can ask for, the number of different care workers each person saw in the last month, alongside late and missed visits. This is a judgement about what should be measured.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE home care guidance recommends that people receiving home care have continuity of care workers so that they are supported by staff they know (NICE NG21, 2015; official guideline).
Staff turnover among care workers in domiciliary care in England is high [N to verify] (Skills for Care workforce data; official statistics).
People receiving home care, and their families, value seeing the same care workers (qualitative or survey evidence; to find, for example Healthwatch or academic studies).

Late and missed visits are the usual monitored measures in home care contracts, and number of distinct workers is not usually reported (commissioning or CQC documents; to find; this claim is the weakest and may need softening).

candidates.working_title: Hours of help, or hours on duty?
candidates.core_insight: Assessments and benefit rules count hours of hands-on care, but many carers of people with dementia describe being on duty around the clock, so a carer assessment should also ask how long the carer can leave the person alone.
candidates.angle: In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia in the year before the person died, half gave at least 46 hours a week of help with daily activities, and more than half said they felt on duty 24 hours a day; the second figure describes supervision that an hours count misses.
candidates.position: When assessing a carer, ask how long they can leave the person on their own and what happens when they do, as well as how many hours of hands-on help they give.
claims_needing_evidence: In 217 family carers of people with dementia, assessed during the year before the person's death, half reported at least 46 hours a week helping with activities of daily living and instrumental activities, and more than half felt 'on duty' 24 hours a day (cohort within a trial; abstract read this session).
In the same study, more than half had ended or reduced paid work because of caring (abstract read this session).

candidates.working_title: Before you give up work to care
candidates.core_insight: Before leaving a job to care for a parent or partner, check the legal rights that might let you keep working, and how to protect your own State Pension record if you do stop.
candidates.angle: The decision to stop work is often made in a crisis, but its costs to the carer last for years; four specific rights and supports in Great Britain are worth checking first.
candidates.position: Leaving paid work to care has long-term costs for the carer. Where possible it should follow a carer's assessment and a conversation with the employer about leave and flexible working, not be decided in the first week of a crisis. This is a judgement; the decision belongs to the carer.
claims_needing_evidence: Since 6 April 2024, employees in England, Scotland and Wales have a right from their first day of employment to up to one week of unpaid carer's leave in any 12 months, to care for a dependant with a long-term care need, which includes needing care because of old age (Carer's Leave Act 2023 and Carer's Leave Regulations 2024; legislation).
Since 6 April 2024, employees in Great Britain can make a request for flexible working from their first day of employment (Flexible Working (Amendment) Regulations 2023; legislation).
Carer's Credit is a National Insurance credit for people caring for at least 20 hours a week who are not getting Carer's Allowance, which helps protect their State Pension record (gov.uk; official).
Carer's Allowance has a weekly earnings limit [N to verify for 2026/27] (DWP; official).
Northern Ireland has different rules on carer's leave (to check before the post names 'UK').

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (look at the smallest practical detail) and the home care worker's viewpoint in the first month led to the wording on a medicine label; kitchen sieve, restaurant kitchens, signposting and redundancy were not used.
candidates.working_title: 'As directed' gives a care worker nothing to follow
candidates.core_insight: Home care workers give medicines according to the written instruction, the medicines chart and their employer's policy, so wording such as 'as directed', or 'when required' without criteria, can lead to doses being missed or given inconsistently.
candidates.angle: Prescribers write instructions as if the patient will remember the consultation; when a care worker gives the medicine, the label and chart are the only instruction they have, and a when-required medicine needs five pieces of information.
candidates.position: For anyone whose medicines are given by care workers, write when-required instructions with the reason, the dose, the minimum interval, the maximum in 24 hours and when to seek advice; do not write 'as directed'.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE guidance on medicines for adults receiving social care in the community recommends clear written directions for medicines that care workers support people to take, including when-required medicines (NICE NG67, 2017; official guideline; exact wording to check).
NICE guidance for care homes recommends that when-required medicines have recorded information on the reason for giving, dose, interval and maximum (NICE SC1, 2014; official guideline; to check).
Care workers administer medicines according to their employer's medicines policy and the care plan, and may not interpret vague directions (CQC guidance on medicines in adult social care; official).
Medication errors, including administration errors, are common in UK care homes (CHUMS study; to check setting and figures).

candidates.working_title: Ask who depends on the patient
candidates.core_insight: Some older people admitted to hospital are the main carer for someone at home, and asking 'Does anyone depend on you for care?' at admission finds a person who may now be alone and unsafe.
candidates.angle: The admission social history asks who helps the patient; the neglected consequence of the admission is the person the patient helps, for example a partner with dementia now alone at home.
candidates.position: Add 'Does anyone depend on you for care?' to the admission history of every older person, and act the same day if the answer is yes, by contacting family or the social work team.

candidates.working_title: Carer's Allowance when you get a State Pension
candidates.core_insight: Carers who get a State Pension usually can't be paid Carer's Allowance as well, but claiming it can still give an 'underlying entitlement' that adds a carer amount to Pension Credit, Housing Benefit or Council Tax Reduction.
candidates.angle: For older carers, the benefit is usually not paid, which leads many to assume there is no point claiming; for those on low incomes the claim itself is what unlocks extra money through other benefits.
candidates.position: Older carers on low incomes should claim Carer's Allowance (Carer Support Payment in Scotland) even when it will not be paid, and ask for a benefits check.
claims_needing_evidence: Because of overlapping benefit rules, Carer's Allowance is not paid on top of a State Pension of the same or higher amount (DWP; official).

A claim still creates an underlying entitlement, which can add a carer amount to Pension Credit, Housing Benefit and Council Tax Reduction (DWP and Age UK or Carers UK factsheets; official and grey literature).
In Scotland, Carer Support Payment has replaced Carer's Allowance and similar rules on State Pension and underlying entitlement apply (Social Security Scotland; official; to confirm).

candidates.working_title: Caring and early death: it was the strained carers
candidates.core_insight: The often-quoted finding that caring shortens life came from spouse carers who reported strain; later population studies found carers as a whole live as long as, or longer than, non-carers, so support should be targeted by asking about strain.
candidates.angle: Both findings hold: in the 1999 US study, only carers who reported strain had higher mortality; the average carer is not the at-risk carer, and the label 'carer' alone does not identify who needs help first.
candidates.position: Ask every carer directly about strain, and offer support first to those who report it; being a carer is not by itself a marker of risk.
claims_needing_evidence: In 392 spouse carers and 427 non-carers aged 66 to 96, carers who reported mental or emotional strain had higher adjusted 4-year mortality than non-carers (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.65); carers without strain did not (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.90) (cohort study; abstract read this session).
Five later population-based studies found lower mortality for carers as a whole than for non-carers, and most carers report some benefit from caring (review; abstract read this session).
The 1999 finding has been widely cited as evidence that caregiving harms physical health (review; abstract read this session).
These are observational findings: people who take on caring may be healthier to begin with, so lower mortality in carers does not show that caring protects health (review full text; PMC copy).
The lower bound of the strain estimate is 1.00, so the finding is at the edge of statistical significance (abstract read; state clearly in the post).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation (test a familiar slogan against the evidence) and the older person's viewpoint in the first hour led to testing 'respite gives carers a break' and asking what the break is like for the person with dementia; jigsaw, choir singing, counting and first impressions were not used.
candidates.working_title: Does respite help? What the trials can and can't tell you
candidates.core_insight: Trials of respite for carers of people with dementia are few and of very low quality, so they have not shown a clear benefit; that is an evidence gap, not proof that breaks don't help, and qualitative research suggests carers rest best when they believe the person is also having a good time.
candidates.angle: Respite is recommended everywhere, and the slogan holds up less well than expected in trials; the qualitative evidence explains why: a break is an outcome in the carer's mind, and it depends on how the person with dementia experiences the service.
candidates.position: Judge a break by two questions: did the carer actually rest, and did the person enjoy it or at least find it tolerable? The lack of trial evidence is not a reason to withhold breaks.
claims_needing_evidence: A Cochrane review found four trials (753 participants) of respite care for people with dementia and their carers, of very low quality, and no significant effects on carer outcomes; the authors said this may reflect the lack of high-quality research rather than a lack of benefit (systematic review; abstract read this session).

A 2026 systematic review of eight studies of respite models found possible improvements in carer outcomes, but four studies were at high risk of bias and four had some concerns (systematic review; abstract read this session).

A concept analysis described respite as both a service and a psychological outcome for the carer, and found that a positive respite experience depends on the carer perceiving benefit for both people (concept analysis; abstract read this session).
A qualitative systematic review found respite services are often under-used and acceptability can be low (review; abstract read this session).

candidates.working_title: Listening to a carer breaches no confidence
candidates.core_insight: GMC guidance says that listening to the concerns of a patient's relatives or carers is not a breach of confidentiality, so refusing to hear a carer on those grounds is a mistake; the patient's consent is needed before sharing their personal information, but not before listening.
candidates.angle: Carers are sometimes turned away with 'I can't discuss the patient'; clinicians can always listen, give general information about a condition and services, and ask the patient what they want shared.
candidates.position: Always listen to carers. Separately, ask the patient what may be shared and with whom, and record the answer where the next clinician will find it.
claims_needing_evidence: GMC confidentiality guidance states that it is not a breach of confidentiality to listen to the concerns of people close to the patient, and that doctors should explain they may not be able to keep the conversation from the patient (official document; paragraph numbers to confirm).
Doctors can give general information about a condition, its treatment and sources of support without disclosing personal information (GMC guidance; official document).
Carers report being excluded from information on confidentiality grounds (survey or qualitative evidence; to find).

candidates.working_title: Your carer's assessment must ask whether you are willing
candidates.core_insight: In England, a carer's assessment must consider whether you are willing to go on caring, as well as whether you are able, and Scotland's adult carer support plan asks the same, so you can say what you will and won't do.
candidates.angle: Many carers feel the question of willingness is closed to them; the law puts it on the assessment form, which supports carers without assuming unlimited unpaid work.
candidates.position: Carers are entitled to set limits. Say them in the assessment, and expect the support plan to take them into account.
claims_needing_evidence: The Care Act 2014 requires a carer's assessment to include whether the carer is able, and willing, to provide care and to continue to do so (Care Act 2014, section 10(5); legislation).

The assessment must also consider the outcomes the carer wants in daily life, and whether they work or wish to, or wish to take part in education, training or recreation (Care Act 2014, section 10; legislation).
An adult carer support plan in Scotland must include the extent to which the carer is able and willing to provide care (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016; legislation; section to confirm).

candidates.working_title: You have a right to be involved in the discharge
candidates.core_insight: In Scotland, and in England, the law requires hospitals to involve unpaid carers in planning the discharge of the person they care for, so you can ask to be part of the planning early and to have your views taken into account.
candidates.angle: Carers often hear about a discharge late; the duty to involve them exists in law in both nations, and naming it gives a carer a firm basis to ask.
candidates.position: Ask the ward early to include you in discharge planning, and ask four questions: when is discharge planned, what help will be needed, what is being asked of me, and who do I call if it goes wrong.
claims_needing_evidence: In Scotland, each health board must take appropriate steps to involve a carer in the discharge of the person they care for and take account of the carer's views (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016; legislation; section to confirm).

candidates.working_title: Relief after the death of the person you cared for
candidates.core_insight: In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them, and their depressive symptoms fell within three months; relief after long, demanding care is a common response, and the study's authors concluded that support was needed most before the death.
candidates.angle: Carers can feel guilty about relief; measured evidence shows it is the majority response in this group, and it shifts attention to support during the caring years.
candidates.position: Relief is a common response after long caring and should be spoken about openly; carer support should be concentrated during the caring years, not only after the death.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72% said the death was a relief to them and more than 90% believed it was a relief to the person who died (study within a trial; abstract read this session).
Carers' depressive symptoms fell to a clinically significant degree within three months of the death, and within a year were substantially lower than while caring (abstract read this session).
The authors concluded that intervention and support were needed most before the death (abstract read this session).

candidates.working_title: Training care home staff: what the WHELD trial changed
candidates.core_insight: In a UK trial in 69 nursing homes, training care staff in person-centred care and social interaction improved residents' quality of life and reduced agitation at lower cost than usual care; the effects were small, and antipsychotic use, already low, did not change.
candidates.angle: Staff training is often treated as a compliance task; here it is an intervention with trial evidence of benefit to residents, delivered through care staff champions.
candidates.position: Training care staff in person-centred care and social interaction should be treated as treatment, with protected time to deliver it, because a trial showed measurable, if small, benefits for residents.
claims_needing_evidence: WHELD was a cluster-randomised trial in 69 UK nursing homes with 847 people with dementia; staff received training in person-centred care and social interaction, with an antipsychotic review, delivered through care staff champions (RCT; abstract read this session).

candidates.working_title: Ask what keeps the carer going
candidates.core_insight: Most carer questionnaires measure strain, but in dementia carers the positive aspects of caring, such as satisfaction, meaning and competence, are linked with lower depression and strain, so a carer assessment should also ask what sustains the carer and protect it.
candidates.angle: An assessment that records only strain misses the things a support plan could protect, such as a shared activity or the sense of doing the job well; the association is cross-sectional, and strain still needs asking about.
candidates.position: A carer assessment should ask what the carer finds worthwhile and what keeps them going, as well as what is hardest, and the support plan should protect those things.

candidates.working_title: The carer's stress predicts the care home move
candidates.core_insight: In a systematic review of 80 studies, consistent predictors of care home admission for people with dementia included the carer's emotional stress, wish to place the person and feeling trapped, alongside the person's cognition, dependency and behaviour, while incontinence did not consistently predict admission.
candidates.angle: The question 'can he stay at home?' is usually answered from the patient's symptoms; the evidence says the carer's state belongs in the same assessment, and one commonly assumed trigger, incontinence, was not a consistent predictor.
candidates.position: When planning whether a person with dementia can stay at home, assess the carer's stress directly and treat it as part of the clinical picture.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of 80 studies found that the most consistent predictors of nursing home admission for people with dementia included severity of cognitive impairment, dependency in basic daily activities, behavioural symptoms and depression (systematic review; abstract read this session).
Carers who reported greater emotional stress, a wish to place the person, and feeling trapped were more likely to move the person to a nursing home (abstract read this session).
Demographic variables, incontinence and service use did not consistently predict admission (abstract read this session).

candidates.working_title: Keeping care staff is part of care quality
candidates.core_insight: In US nursing homes, quality was better when local unemployment was higher, alongside higher staffing and lower staff turnover, and an English hospital study linked staff work experience with older patients' experience of care; this suggests keeping care staff is part of care quality.
candidates.angle: Care quality is usually discussed as individual effort or inspection; observational evidence links it with workforce stability, which is a condition providers and commissioners can measure.
candidates.position: Staff turnover should be reported and treated as a quality measure in care homes and home care. This is a judgement based on observational evidence; it does not depend on any one pay policy.
claims_needing_evidence: In US privately owned nursing homes from 2001 to 2015, higher county unemployment was associated with fewer deficiency citations and better quality measures, with higher nursing staff levels, lower turnover and better retention (panel study; abstract read this session).

In a mixed-methods case study of an English 'Medicine for Older People' service, staff work experiences (demand, control, staffing, leadership) were linked with patients' experience of care (case study; abstract read this session; low survey response rates).
Annual staff turnover for care workers in adult social care in England is [N to verify] (Skills for Care; official statistics).
These are associations; they do not show that reducing turnover alone improves quality (to state clearly in the post).

candidates.working_title: 'They look after their own': what carers report
candidates.core_insight: When carers from minority ethnic groups use fewer services, a systematic review found most of the barriers they described were the same as for all carers, such as low awareness of services and not wanting outsiders involved, with language barriers and poor cultural fit added.
candidates.angle: Low take-up is sometimes read as preference; carers' own accounts point to barriers services can act on.
candidates.position: Low use of carer services by minority ethnic families should prompt services to check awareness, interpreting and cultural fit, rather than being read as a choice not to use them.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of 13 studies found that most barriers to community social care described by minority ethnic carers were potentially relevant to all carers, including not wanting to involve outsiders, not seeing the need, low awareness of services and service availability (systematic review; abstract read this session).

Barriers specific to minority ethnic groups included language barriers and concerns about the cultural appropriateness of services (abstract read this session; describe without reference to religion).
Few studies compared minority and majority ethnic carers directly (abstract read this session).
The phrase 'they look after their own' is used in services to explain low take-up (qualitative literature; to find, or phrase as a belief without claiming frequency).

candidates.working_title: Ask who gives the tablets
candidates.core_insight: For many older people living at home, a family carer manages the medicines, so a medication review that does not include the carer misses the person who knows what is actually taken, refused, missed or hard to give.
candidates.angle: Medication reviews are framed as a conversation between prescriber and patient; systematic reviews describe informal carers taking primary responsibility for medicines management, often with little support, which makes them a participant the review needs.
candidates.position: In any medication review for an older person living at home, ask who sets out and gives the medicines, and invite that person to the review.
claims_needing_evidence: Informal carers often take primary responsibility for medication management for older adults living at home and report challenges with it (mixed-methods systematic review, 16 studies, 2015 to 2025; abstract partly read this session; read results before use).
Family carers of older people with cognitive disorders have specific needs for safe medicines management at home (integrative review; abstract partly read this session).
Carers can report adherence problems and side effects that the patient may not (review results; to confirm).

candidates.working_title: Being there: the rule on visiting and accompanying
candidates.core_insight: In England, since April 2024, a regulation requires hospitals, care homes and hospices to support visiting, and says people attending hospital outpatient and emergency departments should normally be able to have someone with them, so a carer can ask to be present.
candidates.angle: Carers are often treated as visitors who can be sent away; a specific regulation now sets an expectation of presence, with exceptions, and naming it helps a carer ask.
candidates.position: Explanatory: carers in England can ask to accompany the person they care for at hospital appointments and in the emergency department, and to visit in hospitals and care homes, citing the regulation if needed.
claims_needing_evidence: Regulation 9A, visiting and accompanying, came into force in England on 6 April 2024 for CQC-registered providers (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) (Amendment) Regulations; legislation; SI number to confirm).

It requires care homes, hospitals and hospices to facilitate visits to people staying there, and requires that people attending outpatient and emergency departments are not discouraged from being accompanied, with exceptions (CQC guidance on Regulation 9A; official).
Scotland has separate arrangements on care home visiting (Anne's Law provisions; to check current legal status before mentioning).

candidates.working_title: When staying at home costs the carer too much
candidates.core_insight: When a person wants to stay at home and their carer can no longer sustain the care, both interests are real; the law in England and Scotland asks for the person's wishes and the carer's views and willingness to be considered, so the decision should be discussed openly with both.
candidates.angle: These decisions are often framed as safety against guilt; a fairer framing treats the carer's limit as a legitimate fact and the person's wishes as a legitimate fact, and looks for options that have not yet been tried.
candidates.position: The carer's limit is a legitimate reason to change a plan, and the person's wishes still carry weight; before a move, check which options have not been tried, such as more paid care, day care or equipment. This is an ethical judgement.
claims_needing_evidence: In England and Wales, a best-interests decision for a person who lacks capacity must consider the person's past and present wishes and feelings, and take into account the views of anyone engaged in caring for them (Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 4; legislation).

In Scotland, interventions under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 must take account of the adult's wishes and the views of the primary carer and nearest relative (section 1 principles; legislation).
A carer's assessment in England must consider whether the carer is willing to continue caring (Care Act 2014, section 10; legislation).
Carers commonly describe guilt around care home decisions (qualitative evidence; to find, for example a systematic review of family carers' proxy decision-making).
Carer stress and feeling trapped predict care home admission in dementia (Gaugler 2009; abstract read this session), as optional context.
